implementation_notes: C offers neither a messaging runtime nor a standard message header, so the return address is hand-built: the requester creates a private POSIX message queue (mq_open on a name such as /rep_4711), writes that name into the request frame, and blocks in mq_receive; the replier parses the name, mq_open(... O_WRONLY) and mq_send its answer there. The same shape appears on raw sockets, where a server replies to the address returned by recvfrom or to a port encoded in the frame. Nothing validates the address for you, so bounds checking, destination validation and mq_unlink cleanup are part of the pattern's cost.
idiom_name: reply queue name carried in the frame, answered with mq_open/mq_send
pitfalls: The reply queue name is opaque application data: a malformed or oversized field becomes a name/namespace injection into mq_open, so parse and validate it before use.
The queue must outlive the request — unlink it too early and the reply vanishes, never unlink it and stale /rep_* queues accumulate in the kernel namespace.
mq_send blocks when the queue is full unless O_NONBLOCK is set, so one slow requester can stall a single-threaded replier.
